author: TheSpriteWizard
selftext:

Some examples for you guys.

comments.author: Logical_Sail_7167
comments.body: Okay, could you explain what the tool does and what it's used for?

replies.author: TheSpriteWizard
replies.body:
Sure! Sprite Press turns animated 3D models into pixel-art sprites. You import a GLB, GLTF, FBX, or OBJ file, choose the resolution and viewing directions, then adjust the camera, lighting, palette, outlines, and animation frames.

It’s mainly for game developers and artists who want consistent spritesheets or GIFs from 3D assets without drawing every frame and direction by hand.

comments.author: Jolva
comments.body: This is pretty cool. I tried using a 3D model as a reference AI sprite generation before but this looks way more efficient. Cool project.

replies.author: TheSpriteWizard
replies.body: Thanks! That’s the goal. To remove all of the noise from sprite production. I didn’t like having to jump between so many applications for a good result.

replies.author: Choice_Volume4090
replies.body: removing the noise is huge. honestly, half the battle of testing a quick game idea is just getting basic assets and setup out of the way. i've been using combos lately just to throw together a rough playable prototype in the browser to see if a mechanic is even fun before i bother with sprites or opening unity. having a tool like yours to quickly generate consistent sprites once the gameplay loop is actually proven would save so much back-and-forth.

replies.author: TheSpriteWizard
replies.body:
Right. Which was the point I think. Though as of now, I’ve been able to sell 10 models produced by this tool since they come out so well. 

Reducing the headache for newer devs feels like I’m actually helping out instead of just feeding the greed.

comments.author: Hjalm
comments.body:
Amazing. I was just about to set out on a journey to try and create a tool for myself that does exactly this. You're a legend. I'll try it out and see.

If you don't mind me asking, what's going on under the hood here?

replies.author: TheSpriteWizard
replies.body:
Hey, bro! Thanks. 

It’s works in the same way as the SpriteGrid. Its filters the big picture into a smaller picture using an algorithm. That algorithm uses some complex math to keep the output as close to the original as possible. 

It’s not a new concept, as many games do this with a process called “pre-rendering”, it’s can be an expensive process if you don’t know how to do it.
